papers.title: What Counts as Attack Success? Evaluating Harmfulness in Red Teaming LLMs
papers.abstract: Judging whether a model response is harmful requires contextual and normative choices, yet red-teaming studies often delegate this judgment to automated evaluators. We examine how harmfulness criteria are specified in red-teaming research and how they carry through to reported results. Reviewing 76 papers, we find that many adopt their criteria from prior datasets, classifiers, or judge prompts rather than defining harmfulness themselves. Applying evaluators from these papers to identical outputs, we find that they can reach different judgments on the same response, which can change conclusions when comparing models. These differences arise partly because evaluators draw the boundary of harm in different places: some count any response that does not refuse, while others count only output that could plausibly cause harm. We argue that red-teaming studies should state their harmfulness criteria and report how they chose and validated their evaluators to support more reliable measurement and interpretation.

papers.title: Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards for Human-Behavior Simulation
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate survey respondents in social-science research. A useful simulator should predict individual responses, reproduce population response distributions, and capture demographic differences. Common training approaches struggle to balance these goals: exact-match rewards encourage the model to concentrate on the most frequent human response, which is contradictory to the goal of distributional alignment. Meanwhile, aggregate distribution matching can look good even when demographic information is ignored. To this end, we introduce Distributionally-Verifiable Rewards (DVR), a reinforcement-learning reward that uses demographic group distribution gaps to guide individual responses, designed by aligning policy generated frequencies with human response frequencies within each question-group margins. We evaluate the method using the OpinionQA dataset and find that comparing with accuracy-only RLVR, DVR preserves per-response accuracy while reducing JSD by 34.5% in-distribution and 14.6% on held-out questions, with higher DPC point estimates on both splits. Comparing KL-SFT with the demographics-blind marginal further shows that low JSD is insufficient to establish fidelity to population heterogeneity, highlighting that accuracy, distributional fit, and demographic structure should be evaluated together.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Adapting LLMs for English-Swedish Medical Question Answering
papers.abstract: Large language models do well on English medical exams, but less is known about Swedish. This matters most for small open models that hospitals can run locally. To reduce this gap, we first build an item-aligned English-Swedish benchmark from ten medical multiple-choice datasets; each Swedish item keeps the options and answer of its English source. A conservative refinement loop repairs the translations: open models from three families find errors, ground them in a Swedish medical term base, and keep a model-written edit only if blind judges vote for it. On this benchmark, small models lose much more accuracy in Swedish than large ones, especially when they answer without reasoning. Second, we ask whether English data and open teacher models can close this gap. We translate the training data, let teachers write reasoning traces, and fine-tune two small students on gold answers or traces in English, Swedish, or both. Training on reasoning traces that include Swedish closes the gap and lifts the 1.2B student from 23.5\% to 52.0\% in Swedish, slightly above a 20B open model in its fast mode, with a sixth of its memory. We release the benchmark, its edit history, and the code.

papers.title: SnakeTranslate: Weakly Supervised Policy Learning from Offline Parallel Text for Simultaneous Translation
papers.abstract: Adaptive simultaneous translation requires reliable prefix translation and timely READ/WRITE decisions, but ordinary parallel corpora provide no action annotations. We present SnakeTranslate, which adapts loss-derived alignment to sampled causal histories for jointly learning both capabilities. The framework supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on parallel text and on-policy distillation (OPD) with reverse Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence on student-generated translations. At inference, source and target tokens form one append-only interleaved history, enabling incremental decoding with cache reuse. On FLEURS, NTREX128, and WMT24++, our 4B model improves quality--latency trade-offs over streaming policies applied to the same offline-tuned backbone, with further gains from OPD. It also compares favorably with larger translation models at low and moderate latency, while higher-latency quality gaps remain on WMT24++.

papers.title: VidRouteBench: A Benchmark for Budgeted Video-Generation Routing
papers.abstract: Text-to-video generators differ by two orders of magnitude in price, and a cheap configuration of a strong model is often good enough for a prompt. Routing prompts across such arms (model x sampling configuration) should buy quality at fixed budget, but no dataset supports studying it: public video-preference sets contain only closed models, one configuration each. We release VidRouteBench: 16 arms from 7 open families spanning 121x in measured cost ($0.0025-$0.298 per clip), 27,110 clips (1,421 A800-hours) over 1,625 grouped prompts, a quality score frozen after calibration against human preferences (68.7% CV accuracy vs 66.2% for the best single scorer), per-clip scores on 9 identifiable quality dimensions, repeated seeds, an encrypted test split, and a sealed newest family for cold start. The evaluator compares a router against the best prompt-agnostic mixture of arms, not the best single arm. Per-prompt specialisation here is real and predictable (oracle gap 0.642, 47% reproducible across seeds, prompt-arm interaction F=4.47 at p=1.6e-63), unlike LLM-routing arms, where the same pipeline finds none. We then propose OPMU (one probe, many utilities): label a new arm on K probe prompts, predict its 9 dimensions once, and serve any scenario utility by scalarising afterwards. Over 215 utility directions OPMU Pareto-dominates the prompt-agnostic baseline for 94% of directions versus 90% for per-scenario routers, with no per-scenario retraining. Three baselines fail instructively: bag-of-words features lose almost all routing gain in the low-data regime (0.009 vs 0.168); crediting a new arm with its probe average is harmful (-3.32 recovery) although it is the strong baseline on RewardBench-style arms (0.786); Chebyshev scalarisation does not help, our cost-utility front being convex.

papers.title: STEGOGUARD-LM: Evaluating End-to-End Protection Against LLM Covert Channels
papers.abstract: A defense that disrupts hidden messages may still provide little protection if its detector rarely triggers an intervention. We present StegoGuard-LM, a controlled framework for evaluating defenses against covert messages in large language model outputs. We examine token-rank and synonym channels, with Unicode concealment as a structural control, and track messages through detection, intervention, and recovery. Deterministic rewriting prevented full recovery of 103 of 104 synonym-encoded messages when applied unconditionally, but only one when intervention depended on a detector set to limit false alarms. In a four-round replay on a 48-response subset, an attacker selecting from a fixed catalog recovered more bits by switching channels, although paired gains were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Randomized rewriting showed no sustained advantage in this pilot. A more sensitive detector improved protection but modified about one-third of clean responses. These findings show how uneven detection can undermine effective rewriting and why protection must be evaluated alongside attacker adaptation and intervention on legitimate text.

papers.title: From Point Clouds to Engineering Models: Benchmarking Agentic 3D Reconstruction in the Built Environment
papers.abstract: Coding agents can translate 3D measurements into CAD geometry, but reconstructing engineering models for the built environment demands semantic interpretation and consistent construction constraints beyond surface fitting. We formulate scene-level Scan-to-BIM (Building Information Modeling) as an agentic 3D coding task and introduce S2Bench, comprising public and proprietary scans of 128 real-world scenes across five domains, paired with expert-curated reference models spanning diverse spatial scales. A shared framework lets agents measure scans in Python, build class-labeled components in a live CAD/BIM kernel, and iteratively refine their code. We also propose parallel asynchronous collaboration, where a lead delegates versioned tasks, continues modeling while workers execute, and integrates revision-bound proposals. Evaluating five agents and a collaborative team across 1,028 reconstructions shows that scan-to-model residuals directly guide geometric repair, whereas inferring semantic classes and construction relations requires joint geometric, visual, and engineering reasoning that agents struggle to ground and verify. Consequently, the leading agent fits scan geometry closely ($96\%$ coverage within $5\,\text{cm}$) yet reaches only $63\%$ mIoU, and no agent passes all engineering checks on more than $38\%$ of scenes. Coverage and engineering conformance drop with scene scale, whereas running a smaller model as a team improves all three axes with greater coverage gains on larger scenes. The project page is available at https://tumcms.github.io/S2Bench.github.io/

papers.title: Specialized Large Language Models for Markovian Reasoning: Structural Cache Compression, Transition Pretraining, and Dual-Loop Transformers
papers.abstract: Standard autoregressive large language models attend to the growing history of generated tokens, making the key-value (KV) cache a central memory and throughput bottleneck in long-chain reasoning and multi-branch sampling. Yet an important class of reasoning problems is naturally first-order Markovian: the next step depends on a sufficient representation of the current state, rather than on the raw sequence of all earlier steps. We develop a unified design paradigm for Markovian-reasoning specialized large language models. At the cache level, the Markovian state interface transforms history-dependent KV storage into constant-size state transfer with respect to the number of reasoning steps. At the learning level, we reformulate long-chain prediction as independently trainable one-step transition objectives, with explicit state bottlenecks, distillation, invariance, and drift-consistency losses. At the architectural level, we introduce a dual-loop Transformer: an outer loop advances the reasoning state, while an inner recurrent-depth loop allocates adaptive computation to each transition through shared weights and explicit memory tokens or recurrent matrix states. We connect this architecture to a three-region cache, step-relative positions, truncated backpropagation, branch-aware checkpoints, and a transition-centric evaluation protocol. The organizing principle is simple: the optimal reasoning system need not remember everything; it must carry forward exactly what the future needs. This principle opens a path toward specialized reasoning engines whose memory footprint is decoupled from reasoning-chain length.

papers.title: When Video Verifier Scores Mislead: Capability Assessment and Verifier Selection
papers.abstract: Video verifiers judge whether a candidate answer or trajectory agrees with a video, and are themselves chosen by a score. We show that this score depends on two choices in the test, the type of negative and the judgment interface, strongly enough to reverse conclusions about what a model can do and which verifier to deploy. We separate the two with controlled constructions that have exact truth conditions: endpoint-matched negatives, wrong only in their internal states, and a truth-switch test, in which the same two candidates swap correctness between two videos. Under direct judgment, where the verdict is read from answer scores, models that reject a visibly wrong start fall to near chance against endpoint-matched negatives. When the frames disclose each event, writing out reasoning before the answer lifts three of four models from under 10% to 70-100% on the truth-switch test, and staged inputs trace the direct failure to one step, composing events into states. But when the event must first be found, on human-validated natural video, the same change brings no significant gain under a protocol common to all models and can lower accuracy if one candidate denies that the event occurs. The negative type also changes which verifier is selected: one chosen on event-denial negatives is 8.9 points less accurate against negatives that keep the event and change a detail, the errors a generator mostly makes, and recovers about half as much accuracy when it reranks that generator's answers. A verifier should be evaluated on the errors it will face, and neither a low direct score nor a gain from reasoning should be read as a property of the model alone.

papers.title: Feedback-Driven Prompt Refinement for Educational AI: Affective Trajectory Estimation and Bloom's Taxonomy Classification
papers.abstract: Contribution: This study has shown that a shared prompt-refinement procedure, guided by distinct affective and cognitive feedback signals, can improve held-out reference agreement and multi-label classification while reducing affective-generation variability without executor parameter updates. Background: Industry 4.0 has increased demand for personalized technical education across interconnected computing and engineering domains, while prompt sensitivity and generation variability have complicated dependable interpretation of instructional dialogue and learning outcomes. Research Questions: The study has examined whether task-specific feedback can improve affective-reference agreement, generation consistency, and cognitive classification without updating executor parameters. Methodology: A secondary language model has revised executor prompts using executor-output discrepancies against model-generated affective references for four dialogues and annotated Bloom labels for 70 learning outcomes; separate sets of 100 EduTalk conversations and 1,000 outcomes have supported held-out comparisons. Small refinement sets, unvalidated affective references, and absent learner-outcome measures have constrained interpretation. Findings: Affective mean absolute error has decreased from 0.742 to 0.702 and mean generation standard deviation from 0.307 to 0.238, while Bloom micro-F1 has increased from 0.687 to 0.893 and exact-match subset accuracy from 0.418 to 0.636. These findings have supported prompt refinement as a candidate approach for developing adaptive technical instruction, while its effects on workforce learning remain to be established.

papers.title: Language Model Harnesses can be Compositional Generalizers
papers.abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are post-trained and deployed as agents inside a "harness", but standard harness designs accumulate context that the neural network is forced to generalize to, making training for long-horizon tasks expensive and time-consuming. We study an alternative emerging path: training inherently neurosymbolic LM harnesses, which externalize and manage context programmatically to compose existing LM capabilities. We hypothesize that training around these harnesses can offer a better return on compute by enabling compositional generalization, as they can learn to decompose complex problems so that every observation their neural LM receives is locally in-distribution, even when the full task is novel. We find that harnesses like the Recursive Language Model (RLM) learn such decompositions readily under reinforcement learning post-training: (1) we demonstrate that training only on short tasks can generalize to tasks 2-64$\times$ longer while the base neural LM improves less, and (2) training on one domain transfers to novel domains that share latent structure. On messier, complex tasks, we find that we can target individual LLM calls within a harness by generating and training on easier, synthetically generated surrogate environments with fake tool / sub-calls, a technique we call surrogate harness training. From this finding, we train RLM-27B on synthetic data, and show it improves Qwen3.8-27B in the same RLM harness on a hard suite of long-context tasks like CTC-Bench and ExpertLongBench by 26.9% on average while using $\sim$2$\times$ fewer tokens at inference time. Finally, we show that harnesses can compose over these newly learned decompositions using recursive sub-harness calls.

papers.title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration
papers.abstract: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.

papers.title: When Tools Fail, Agents Fabricate: Silent Failure and Verification-First Oversight in Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents must recover when a tool call fails, by retrying, switching tools, or revising their plan. We study how agents fail when tools fail, using RetryRealistic, a sandboxed yet realistic testbed for controlled fault injection in which agents operate on a real OS filesystem with genuine permission enforcement, SQLite databases, a deterministic local HTTP server, and a constrained shell, across 8 tools, 9 fault types with controlled persistence, and 30 multi-step tasks. Evaluating four agents over 2,100 faulted runs against ground truth, we find that recovery is unreliable (19-68% correct) and frequently silent: 6-26% of runs end in a confident fabrication, a wrong answer asserted as fact. The failure mode is governed more by the fault type than by the model: faults that return partial data drive fabrication (up to 38%), while hard denials drive honest failure. The mechanism is what we call silent ingestion: the agent accepts faulted data as valid on first contact without retrying or flagging the problem, then builds a fabricated answer on top of it. We show that fabrication is reducible: a verification-first Monitor, grounding checks in structured tool outputs and issuing corrective directives rather than hard blocks, raises correct recovery from 45.6% to 56.3% and cuts fabrication from 17.3% to 10.8%. Removing chain-of-thought increases fabrication (+8.3pp), so deliberation guards against silent ingestion. We release RetryRealistic, the fault-injection toolkit, and all annotated traces at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/RetryRealistic

papers.title: Grammar-as-a-Draft: More Tokens per Speculative Decoding Step on Grammar-Constrained Structured Outputs
papers.abstract: Under structured outputs (JSON schemas, regexes, tool calls), speculative drafters do not see the grammar constraint and repeatedly propose invalid keys, delimiters, and indentation, while the grammar engine already knows which tokens must come next. We present Grammar-as-a-Draft (GaaD), which treats the grammar as a second drafter. Before each verify step, the scheduler merges the drafter's proposal with grammar-forced tokens into one draft row: matching tokens stay as GRAMMAR, the proposal is cut where it leaves the forced path, and forced tokens fill the rest of a row wider than the drafter's proposal. The verify step accepts GRAMMAR drafts without computing their logits, composing with any drafter with no new kernels or compilation on the critical path. Because grammars fix text rather than tokens, committing canonical forced tokens changes the output distribution relative to grammar-masked target decoding. We implement GaaD in vllm-torchtpu and an independent Rust serving runtime, evaluating on TPU v7x with MTP, DFlash, and n-gram drafters on a JSON character-profile benchmark. GaaD raises average acceptance length from 2.06 to 5.43 (MTP, Qwen3.5-0.8B), 1.99 to 5.31 (MTP, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), 1.57 to 4.13 (DFlash, Qwen3-4B), and 1.30 to 3.64 (n-gram, Qwen3-4B), decoding 2.66-2.81x faster at batch size 1 and 1.14-1.70x at batch size 64. In Rust, MTP+GaaD is 2.23x faster on Qwen3.5-0.8B, 2.02x on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8, and 1.22x at 128 concurrent requests. Under mixed traffic (25-50% structured), GaaD finishes the workload 1.03-1.23x sooner (structured requests 2.2-3.2x sooner) while plain-text TPOT rises 7-42%. We also show grammar-masked greedy decoding can pick non-canonical tokenizations, so GaaD can yield different valid outputs that an fp32 reference finds equally likely.

papers.title: Contrastive On-Policy Distillation via Dual-Branch Supervision
papers.abstract: For on-policy distillation (OPD), more capable models are a natural choice as teachers. However, higher task performance does not necessarily imply greater teachability. A controlled token intervention study suggests that even a model weaker than the student can serve as an informative contrastive reference. Building on this observation, we propose Contrastive On-Policy Distillation (cOPD), which provides dual branch supervision by contrasting strong teacher, weak teacher, and student predictions at student generated prefixes. Our analysis explains how this three way comparison helps select token candidates associated with better or worse reasoning outcomes under an idealized model. We evaluate cOPD across diverse teacher student configurations spanning different training stages, parameter scales, and model families, on tasks including mathematical reasoning, instruction following, and question answering with abstention. cOPD achieves the best or top-tier performance among the evaluated baselines across all three tasks, improving overall Pass@16 on mathematical reasoning by up to 7.51\% over the strongest baseline. Further analyses show that cOPD suppresses undesirable response patterns and suggest that it facilitates exploration.

papers.title: Taking the PULSE of Enterprise Workflows: Evaluating Persistent Project-State Understanding
papers.abstract: Enterprise agents must maintain an up-to-date understanding of work distributed across heterogeneous artifacts, evolving over time, and unevenly visible to different collaborators. We formulate this challenge as persistent project-state understanding (PPSU) and introduce PULSE, a benchmark of 1,573 questions over 30 enterprise project histories. PULSE constructs deterministic, time-indexed project state and documented collaborator views from source-linked records, and evaluates three families of questions: open loops, project evolution, and view gaps. Across retrieval agents, graph- and memory-augmented retrieval, long-context, and oracle conditions, we find substantial headroom for current systems. Retrieval and extraction account for the largest share of the gap, but providing explicit project state on top of gold evidence yields further substantial gains, showing that PPSU cannot be reduced to retrieval alone. Further analysis shows that questions requiring information to be reconciled across multiple parts of the project history remain difficult even when the relevant evidence is provided, while project-state synthesis and perspective conditioning remain persistent challenges. These results motivate enterprise agents that explicitly maintain and reconcile temporally grounded state across sources, actors, and time.

papers.title: Language models compress human preference geometry while political structure remains prompt-sensitive
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to construct synthetic publics. Prior work has documented errors in individual responses, population heterogeneity, and prompt robustness, but whether these failures reflect a common loss of fidelity or distinct properties of synthetic populations remains unclear. We tested this using matched pairwise policy choices from 1,991 Chilean, 843 French, and 434 Brazilian adults replayed through three open-weight model families. Across a 27-condition Chilean grid and cross-country factorial replications, no condition jointly reproduced individual choices, population heterogeneity, and political organization. The most consistent result was compression of the latent preference space: synthetic participant variance was only 0.4-10.5% of the corresponding human reference in the primary comparisons and remained below human variance in all 270 matched refits. Political structure was much more sensitive to how choices were elicited. Reversing proposal position changed 12.3-31.2% of decoded choices. Explicitly labeling the endpoints of the numeric left-right self-placement scale changed 20.5-28.1% of choices and moved an independent proposal-level measure of left-right cleavage toward the human pattern in all three settings. Yet matched agreement improved by only 3.1-4.2 percentage points and participant geometry remained compressed. In Chile, the same intervention compressed the synthetic population further. These results separate political legibility from population fidelity: language models can recover salient political divisions while failing to preserve the breadth of human preference variation. Synthetic-public fidelity is therefore a property of the checkpoint, prompt, and setting, not of a checkpoint alone, and must be evaluated separately at individual, population, and political-structure levels.

papers.title: Muted Distillation: Sealing Reasoning from Teacher Unlocks Token-Efficient Agents
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is commonly adopted as one of the components in post-training of large language models (LLMs), but in multi-turn agentic tasks we find that the student model increases their reasoning lengths after training. Our empirical analysis shows that the reasoning token lengths is affected by how much the student can distract the teacher's scores. We introduce Muted Distillation (MD), a simple variant of OPD that hides the student's reasoning from the teacher, so the teacher judges what the student does without the interference of student's reasonings. MD takes a few lines of code and adds no extra data or hyperparameters. On the knowledge-work benchmarks OfficeQA Pro and SpreadsheetBench, it reduces output tokens per episode by 57\% and 53\% compared with standard OPD, making the student more concise than it was before training. At the same time, it matches OPD's accuracy on OfficeQA Pro and improves pass@1 by 4.8 points on SpreadsheetBench.

papers.title: Digital Knockoffs
papers.abstract: Social simulations often use language model agents to represent people who differ on several measurable traits. However, describing a trait profile in a prompt does not guarantee the agent will express each trait at its intended level. We propose a method that calibrates agents to multidimensional profiles using activation steering: (i) extract steering directions for each trait, (ii) learn a shared mapping from steering strengths to measured trait scores, and (iii) search for a steering intervention for each target. We use Bayesian optimization for this search and evaluate the method on the Big Five personality scores of 500 OpenPsychometrics respondents. In each of five rounds, the assigned interventions yield lower mean absolute error across respondents than the prompting and steering baselines. Further, the model's responses to a given intervention yield the same trait profile regardless of whose target motivated it, so a poor match for one respondent can be the best match for another. When we match each respondent to the closest profile found across all tested interventions, Bayesian optimization yields 16.6% lower mean absolute error than uniform random search at the same evaluation budget. Our method thus offers a way to build social agents whose measured traits dovetail with those of the people they seek to represent. Whether this closer fit translates to improved predictions of downstream behavior remains an open question.

papers.title: Digital Twins for Multi-Agent Systems: When to Trust, What to Change
papers.abstract: Digital twins of agent networks need to flag unreliable forecasts and help users choose interventions. Both decisions depend on what happens over several steps: an error can spread through the network, and an edit whose trajectory is easy to predict may still yield a poor collective outcome. We ask when information about error propagation improves failure detection and whether a learned twin can select effective network edits despite imperfect forecasts. We propose Propagation-Aware Validation for Networked Digital Twins (PAV-Twin). Its monitor combines Jacobian-based propagation features with recent errors and ensemble disagreement to estimate the risk that a forecast exceeds an error threshold. Its planner simulates each candidate edit and ranks the edits by their predicted collective outcomes. In simulations, the monitor gained 0.13 in area under the precision-recall curve on larger oscillator networks with familiar topologies and 0.09 on larger networks with held-out topologies, relative to a graph baseline without propagation features. Gains were small in contractive consensus. Giving the graph baseline the same features narrowed the gap. In a separate planning study, ensemble simulation recovered about 99% of the possible improvement over random intervention selection in oscillators and nearly all of it in consensus. With a simplified oscillator twin, selecting by predicted outcome also gave lower regret than selecting by trajectory fidelity. These results show when propagation features help flag unreliable forecasts and why the quality of intervention choices should be measured directly.

papers.title: SupportChain: Trace-Calibrated Aggregation of Quote-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Multi-Hop RAG with Small Readers
papers.abstract: Strong results in multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering come from graph indexes read by models of 70B parameters or more, and building such an index calls a large language model over the whole corpus. We present SupportChain, which splits a question into hops, binds each hop's answer to a sentence quoted from a retrieved passage, estimates how reliable each execution is from its own trace, and merges several executions by the support of their answers, the pooled reliability of the executions that agree, stopping once support is high enough. With a 9B reader under the HippoRAG~2 protocol, SupportChain reaches 63.0 F1 on MuSiQue, above the best earlier result of 59.2, which used a 20B reader. With the same reader and embedder, it is significantly better than HippoRAG~2 on all five datasets, by up to 17.2 F1, and it builds no index. Merging by support is significantly better than majority voting, and than letting the reader choose among the candidates, on three of the five datasets and level with both on the other two. The reliability model needs only 100 answered training questions.

papers.title: Information Access and Gain-Loss Framing in Six Large Language Models and Human Decision Makers
authors: Jeremy M. Gernand (The Pennsylvania State University)
papers.abstract: A risky choice can be described by what will be saved or what will be lost, and people often choose differently depending on that wording. We test whether six large language models (LLMs) show this gain-loss framing effect, and whether it shrinks when they can first read more about the options. GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3 235B and Llama 4 Maverick made 11,519 choices across four risk scenarios, each in its original wording, two paraphrases and a mirrored version in the opposite wording. Before choosing, a model could open up to 0, 2, 3 or 4 of seven information cards. With no cards, all six models showed large framing effects: the share choosing the safe option was 27 to 79 percentage points lower under loss than under gain wording. The gap was smaller at 2 cards than with no cards in every model. Against a 10-point threshold set in our analysis plan, GPT-4.1 fell within it at 4 cards and Qwen3 only at 2 cards; in the plan's pooled comparison over all versions, GPT-4.1 was within it from 2 cards and GPT-4o from 3. GPT-4o-mini and Llama 4 Maverick kept gaps of 28 to 66 points with cards, and for GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3 the gap grew again from 2 to 4 cards. Part of the drop from 0 to 2 cards may reflect a change in prompt format, and most card content counted against the risky option, which may favor the safe choice. In an exploratory comparison with 198 students who saw the same scenarios and cards but opened cards one at a time and chose how many, decisions made after opening 0 or 1 cards showed a 19-point difference between the gain scenarios, asked first, and the loss scenarios, asked later, and no clear difference appeared in decisions made after opening more, though this design cannot show that cards reduced framing in people. With these cards, in the balanced comparison 17 of 18 card gaps were below the model's no-card gap, but few were within the threshold.

papers.title: BIRD-Persona: A Persona-Aware Benchmark for SQL and pandas Analytics Code Generation
papers.abstract: Production text-to-code systems use large language models to turn natural-language analytics requests into executable SQL and pandas code. Existing benchmarks cover both tasks but do not isolate when performance diverges between them. We introduce BIRD-Persona, a persona-stratified extension of BIRD-Python that adds novice and expert rewrites to tasks with matched SQL and pandas ground truth, along with schema variants and task-structure annotations. Across 1,534 tasks, nine models, and 245,592 evaluations, SQL outperforms pandas for eight of nine systems. The gap varies by condition: expert, schema-explicit prompts improve both paradigms but help SQL more; schema representations have mixed, model-dependent effects; and selected-column burden widens the gap while subqueries do not. By making user phrasing a controlled benchmark dimension, BIRD-Persona supports persona-aware and paradigm-aware evaluation of natural-language analytics systems. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/optum-cognition-lab/BIRD-Persona.

papers.title: From Reward Engineering to Data-Centric Reinforcement Learning for Effective Agentic Visual Tool Use
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly use external visual tools to acquire evidence during reasoning, yet learning when to invoke these tools remains challenging. Existing tool-use reinforcement learning (RL) methods often rely on call-contingent rewards to encourage beneficial tool use, but such reward engineering can distort the task objective and lead to degenerate calling behaviors. We argue that effective tool-use learning requires identifying not merely which questions are difficult, but which failures are attributable to missing visual evidence and can therefore be corrected through tool observations. We propose AOVO, a data-centric framework that enables MLLMs to learn effective tool use through perception attribution and policy-adaptive data sampling (PADS), without introducing tool-specific rewards. It counterfactually probes the model's reasoning states to identify observation-sensitive questions, distinguishing them from reasoning-dominated ones. PADS then periodically estimates category-level observation effects from recent policy rollouts and dynamically reallocates the training distribution toward questions where visual observations provide informative learning signals, while optimizing solely for final-answer correctness. Experiments across diverse visual perception and multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over competitive tool-use MLLMs, with causal analysis further validating the data-centric perspective for learning effective visual tool use.

papers.title: Tool-to-Self: Internalizing Visual Tool Capabilities via Scaffolded Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) increasingly rely on external visual tools to access fine-grained visual evidence, but repeated tool execution incurs substantial inference overhead and deployment dependencies. Moreover, conventional tool-use RL can improve visual-task performance, yet the resulting tool gains are often unstable. Motivated by this, we propose Tool-to-Self (T2S), a tool-scaffolded reinforcement learning framework that turns external visual tools into temporary training scaffolds. T2S cold-starts tool-use ability and observation prediction from tool-repairable examples, then progressively anneals tool execution on a per-tool basis during RL. By combining answer-correctness and observation-consistency rewards with privileged on-policy self-distillation from actual tool observations, T2S effectively teaches the model both to reproduce tool outputs and to reason from them. Experiments across diverse visual perception and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over both explicit tool-use models and implicit zooming models while enabling tool-free inference with reduced latency.

papers.title: Modeling Perceived Promptness in Simultaneous Interpreting from Quality, Structure, and Timing Signals
papers.abstract: Simultaneous interpreting requires interpreters to convey the source accurately while keeping pace with it in real time. Timing measures such as segment-onset delay capture part of this requirement, but may not fully reflect how professional evaluators judge promptness. We investigate whether these judgments can be explained by timing alone or whether the interpreted output provides additional information. Our dataset contains 622 Chinese-English and English-Chinese segments from 16 source speeches and seven interpreters. Two senior professional interpreters rated each segment for language quality (LQ), expressiveness (EXP), and perceived latency (LAT), which we also refer to as professional promptness. On held-out source speeches, onset delay alone achieves a Pearson correlation of r = .318 with LAT ratings. Combining predicted LQ and EXP with delay improves the correlation to r = .475. Lexical and structural features provide a stronger signal, reaching r = .632 when combined with delay and r = .658 when predicted quality is also included. These results suggest that professional promptness judgments reflect properties of the interpreted output beyond when the interpreter begins speaking. The additional contribution of predicted quality over structural features, however, is modest. Although the two evaluators differ in how strongly quality relates to LAT, cross-evaluator predictions remain positively correlated with LAT ratings. The overall pattern also holds when each interpreter is held out in turn.

papers.title: CLASP: Deciding Structure and Claims Before Decoding for Whole-Slide Pathology Report Generation
papers.abstract: Whole-slide pathology report generation has advanced through stronger slide encoders, retrieved knowledge, and, recently, slide-level multimodal LLMs. However, these generators leave every report-level choice to the decoder: how long the report is, how it is organised, and which findings it states and where. On the standard PathText-BRCA benchmark, we find that these choices dominate n-gram overlap, as reports from the query's hospital selected without learning approach the state of the art, while decoders under-generate and fall back to the most frequent findings. We present CLASP, a decide-then-decode generator that makes these choices explicitly, once per slide. Before decoding, an Exemplar Structure Prior (ESP) takes the sentence plan and length from reports of image-similar cases, a Calibrated Claim Decision (CCD) selects the findings from calibrated slide posteriors, and a Claim-to-Sentence Placement (CSP) assigns each finding to a planned sentence. A Plan-Conditioned Decoder (PCD), refined by structure-anchored sequence training, then writes the report under these decisions. With 35M parameters, CLASP outperforms retrained report generators and slide-level LLMs of up to 7B parameters, matches the strongest published results, and generalises to lung cancer from unseen hospitals. Its decisions change what the reports state, not only their length, transfer to an LLM decoder, and can withhold what H&E cannot show: withholding receptor status leaves 23% fewer contradictions with clinical records than the same network without decisions.

papers.title: MedCoast: Semantic Abstraction of Reasoning Trajectories for Test-Time Biomedical Question Answering
papers.abstract: Biomedical question answering often requires multi-step reasoning under limited inference budgets. While test-time search methods such as Tree-of-Thought can improve reasoning performance, directly searching over free-form language is computationally expensive and highly redundant, as many reasoning trajectories contain semantically equivalent intermediate steps expressed in different surface forms. We introduce MedCoast, an offline-to-online reasoning framework that converts sampled chain-of-thought trajectories into a compact space for structured process supervision. Offline, we recursively cluster semantically similar reasoning steps under shared prefixes to construct an abstract reasoning tree that captures recurring clinical reasoning patterns. We then derive node-level supervision from progress toward correct solutions, and train a lightweight process reward model (PRM) to evaluate partial reasoning states. At inference time, the learned critic guides test-time exploration by prioritizing promising reasoning prefixes. Across seven biomedical QA benchmarks, MedCoast often improves over self-consistency under fixed inference budgets, with gains of up to 15 points. Despite using a reward model more than 50 times smaller, MedCoast achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art reward models in several settings, highlighting its potential for resource-constrained biomedical reasoning.

papers.title: CLOSE: A Calibrated Label-free Online Self-Evaluating Verifier for Object Hallucination in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Vision-language models frequently describe objects absent from the image because of language priors. Yet the model itself is already a strong judge of its own output: asked separately whether an object is present, it rejects 44%-62% of its hallucinations, and its yes probability reaches an AUROC of 0.90-0.95 without training. This judgment, however, is not directly usable: (1) its probabilities lack a common scale across models; (2) for the remaining 38%-56%, the model still answers yes with probabilities that overlap those of real objects, so no threshold separates them. We therefore propose CLOSE, a Calibrated Label-free Online Self-Evaluating verifier that enforces this judgment during generation. Its threshold is a quantile of a memory rather than a probability and thus depends only on ranks; the memory is cold-started from unlabeled images and updated online. A scorer self-trained on pseudo-labels from four hidden-state signals is fused with self-asking by rank to separate what self-asking leaves mixed. Refused objects are rolled back and banned through a laddered back-off, and a recognition table intercepts their reappearance under other wordings. On COCO, refusing 20% and 40% of object mentions reduces the CHAIRs of LLaVA-1.5-7B by 42% and 87% (F1 +1.9 and -6.1 points); refusing 20% and 35% reduces the reachable hallucinations of Qwen3-VL-8B (official counts minus CHAIR-script miscounts) by 79% and 96% (F1 +0.5 and -5.3). An external vocabulary further extends the check beyond the official vocabulary.

papers.title: Reducing Permutation Sensitivity in Multimodal Large Language Models via Shared Positions and Attention-Only Distillation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on improving permutation robustness while preserving accuracy. First, we categorize permutation bias phenomena into four representative scenarios. Then, we take the multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) dataset as an example under text-option reordering scenario to analyze the root cause of permutation bias. Based on this root cause analysis and set encoding strategy, we investigate shared positions with blocked cross-unit attention (SP-B) and extend this design to bidirectional cross-unit attention (SP-V) for modality exchange. However, these structural changes may reduce predictive accuracy. To recover model capability across different scenarios under the SP structure, an attention-only distillation from frozen native models is proposed. Shared positions reduce permutation sensitivity, and attention-only distillation improves accuracy under the shared-position structure. Across all three models, our method is comparable to or better than majority voting in macro-average all-permutation accuracy, and outperforms supervised fine-tuning by 1.95-4.20 percentage points. This work provides valuable insight into permutation bias mitigation and model capability recovery.
